assessment.nobel_worthiness: A new measurement capability: the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock combines the stability of many atoms with the Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation of trapped ones, pushing fractional uncertainty to the 1e-18 level. This is the kind of precision-measurement advance that opens new observations (relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches, a future redefinition of the second).
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first demonstrations; Ye's group drove the strontium clocks to record accuracy and stability and ties to the frequency-comb and ultrastable-laser work. Two laureates is a clean configuration, though Hall and Hänsch were already recognised in 2005 for the comb and others (e.g. Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom) built on the clocks.
assessment.maturity: Many independent clocks (Sr, Yb) at several institutes have been compared at 1e-18 and are used in international comparisons, so confirmation is strong and the interpretation is stable. Timing looks right, although the redefinition of the second is still pending.
uncertainties: I have not independently verified the details of priority between the early Katori proposal and parallel work on lattice clocks in other groups.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the redefinition of the second to reinforce the impact is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms became a general-purpose precision sensor for gravity, gravity gradients, rotation and the fine-structure constant, with direct relevance to metrology and tests of fundamental physics. It carries a measurement-first character that I weight heavily.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard demonstrated early atom interferometers with gratings and light; Bordé provided the theoretical framework and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer; Kasevich demonstrated the high-precision gravimeter and gradiometer and the large-momentum-transfer approach. Chu's overlapping contribution was already honoured in 1997 and Ramsey-type work complicates a clean line, but three names is workable.
assessment.maturity: Field gravimeters are commercially available and long-baseline instruments are under construction. Independent confirmation across many groups is solid, although the fundamental-physics reach (equivalence principle, gravitational waves) is still prospective.
uncertainties: Credit between the early grating/optical interferometers and the later atomic-fountain devices is spread across more people than three.
Could be seen as partly overlapping with the 1997 laser-cooling recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong coherent coupling between a superconducting artificial atom and a single microwave photon routine, and became the architecture of leading quantum processors and of quantum-limited readout. The coherence-time and fidelity progress is quantitatively impressive and has enabled other work across the field.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 proposal and its first experiment; Wallraff (strong coupling, Nature 2004) and Schoelkopf (transmon, dispersive readout, cavity-based control) are the experimental drivers, and Blais the principal theorist. Girvin and Devoret are notable omissions in the supplied names and the superconducting-circuit area was recognised in 2025, which makes the allocation delicate.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, with many independent groups and industrial platforms. Its closeness to the recent circuit-based prize is a timing question rather than a doubt about the science.
uncertainties: Overlap with the most recent superconducting-circuit prize could make the committee reluctant to return to the same platform so soon.
Girvin is not among the credited names, so the fair credit split is not fully supportable from the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and coherent control of single defect spins (NV centres and relatives) created nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry and biosensing at ambient conditions. As someone who works with spins and coherence in crystals, I value the combination of single-spin physics and a measurement tool that is now used in biology, materials and geoscience.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup demonstrated optical detection of single NV spins; Awschalom pushed coherent control and semiconductor defect spins; Lukin contributed the quantum-register and nanoscale-sensing proposals and demonstrations; Walsworth is credited as well and the allocation is unsettled. Several other groups (Jelezko, Hanson, Yacoby) are not in the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Widely reproduced and still growing rapidly. Real quantitative sensing applications exist but the field is not yet settled on a single canonical discovery.
uncertainties: The decisive-discovery claim is spread over many groups and years, and Jelezko/Hanson are not in the credited strings.
Practical sensitivity beyond proof-of-principle applications is still being established.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Prediction of flat bands at the magic angle followed by the experimental observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened an entire field of tunable moire quantum matter. This is a clear case of theory and experiment each making a decisive step and of enabling a large body of follow-up work.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the 2011 prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the 2018 discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity (with Cao, whose name is not in the supplied credit). Andrei's earlier STM evidence of flat bands is a rival claim to a share.
assessment.maturity: Replicated in many labs, though the superconductivity mechanism and some transport details remain debated. Timely, perhaps slightly early for a final verdict on the pairing physics.
uncertainties: The mechanism for superconductivity is unresolved.
Allocation involves Eva Andrei's earlier STM work and the first author of the key experiments, who is not among the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices allow controlled realisation of Hubbard models, with the superfluid-Mott transition, single-site imaging with quantum gas microscopes and now quantum simulation of magnetism. It has changed how many-body physics is explored experimentally.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch proposed the Mott-insulator realisation; Greiner and Bloch carried out the Mott transition experiment and developed the quantum gas microscope; Esslinger and Cirac are also defensible. Five names compete for three slots, so the allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Mature in methods; the quantitative advantage over classical simulation in open problems is still emerging.
uncertainties: Credit is broad (Hänsch, Esslinger, Cirac, Kasevich, Jaksch) so any triple is arguable.
Part of the underlying cooling and BEC work was already prized in 1997 and 2001.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Rydberg blockade supplies a controllable strong interaction between single atoms, and optical tweezer arrays give programmable, scalable qubit registers, now used for quantum simulation and gate-based processing. The experimental progress in fidelity and array size is substantial.
assessment.attribution: The blockade proposals come from Jaksch/Zoller and Lukin; Saffman et al. proposed gates, and Browaeys (with Grangier) demonstrated the blockade at the single-atom level, while Lukin's group built the large programmable arrays. The decisive allocation between theory, blockade demonstration and array platforms is unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Still maturing; error-corrected logic with neutral atoms is recent and the field is moving quickly, so recognition may be somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Possibly premature, with the best demonstrations being only a few years old.
Whether the Nobel unit is the blockade or the programmable arrays is unclear, and Saffman is left out of my three.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state with time-reversal-protected edge states and its experimental observation in HgTe wells established topological band insulators as a new class of matter. It is a clean theory-plus-experiment story with lasting conceptual impact.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the original prediction, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposed HgTe, and Molenkamp's group observed the edge conduction; Hasan is credited for three-dimensional topological insulators. Fu and Kane's three-dimensional work and Zhang's death complicate the picture; the supplied credit supports a Kane, Mele, Molenkamp triple but at the cost of leaving out the 3D discovery.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by ARPES and transport; the field is established, though practical devices are still scarce, which weakens the measurement-impact argument I care about.
uncertainties: The 2D versus 3D split and the missing credited names (Bernevig, Zhang, Fu) make allocation difficult.
Overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases.
